notes: \cpara{Opens with the claim that the author remembers the exact moment the journey as a rationalist began.}
\cpara{Says the journey began not with books, whose lessons seemed obvious, but with seeing a great flaw in one's own skills and wanting new ones.}
\cpara{Sets the scene: at fifteen the author was going over a ``pleasantly self-righteous'' memory from age six or seven. The post grants that the memory is vague.}

\cpara{Tells the event: a teenage counselor proposed a game in which the boys spanked each other, the author refused, and was sent to sit in the corner. The parenthesis hints at a suspicion about the counselor and leaves it unstated.}
\cpara{Gives the meaning the memory had come to carry. It has two parts: a refusal ``to take joy in hurting others,'' and a refusal ``to play a negative-sum game.''}

\cpara{The correction. Its one piece of evidence, that a seven-year-old knew nothing of the Prisoner's Dilemma, rules out only the second part of the flattering reading, the stand against negative-sum games. It does not rule out the first part, that the child did not want to hurt others, which needs no game theory. The post replaces both with ``I didn't want to get hurt.''}

\cpara{What settles the choice between the two motives is introspection: a sense that the ``real memory'' had always been there, glimpsed and avoided. The post has just shown that a confident reading of this memory could be wrong. It does not ask whether the new reading could be wrong too, or say how a truth recovered in this way can be told from a new story that feels true.}
\cpara{States the resolution drawn from the episode: learn the feeling of pushing an unwanted truth into a corner, and notice it every time.}

\cpara{Names the skill after Orwell's doublethink. The gloss matches Orwell. In \textsc{Nineteen Eighty-Four} doublethink includes the power ``to forget whatever it was necessary to forget \ldots\ and above all, to apply the same process to the process itself,'' and is defined as ``holding two contradictory beliefs in one's mind simultaneously.''}
\cpara{Claims singlethink as the author's first new skill, and grants that it may not be original ``in the sense of academic priority.''}
\cpara{Says that the mechanisms by which the brain pushes things aside are many, and are found by experience or by reading.}

\cpara{Ends by saying that the first ``broom'' swept ``quite a few corners.'' No second corner is described. The post's one example is the discovery that started the practice, so the claim that the practice worked rests on the author's word.}
